lines.text: Chapter four, section two. Hand reading on the flop to guide range construction on the turn.
Before you can barrel a turn effectively, you need a sensible picture of what your opponent's flop range actually looks like.
Return to the king of diamonds, eight of diamonds, eight of clubs scenario, where the button opens and the big blind defends.
The big blind called a small c-bet on the flop, so we can infer that her range is condensed: mostly pairs, some flush draws, and probably some ace-high with backdoor equity.
She almost certainly folded her worst hands, and she probably did not check-raise, which discounts, but does not eliminate, monster hands like trips.

You should be aware that a real player may not defend exactly like the solver: some love to slowplay trips, some are terrified of getting counterfeited and just call, and some will not defend queen-jack of clubs at all.
Without a read, though, you cannot assume any of these deviations without opening yourself to exploitation.
Equilibrium hand reading gives you a reasonable prior for the opponent's range, and your turn strategy should perform sensibly against any distribution that is close to it.

The key habit is that equilibrium play is robust: even if your opponent slowplayed her trips and shows up with a stronger-than-expected range, your best-response strategy still does no worse than break even against her, and it prevents her from doing any better than she would have by playing correctly.
Hand reading is not about guessing the exact hand; it is about narrowing the range to a shape you can attack the turn against.
